The video shows a person wearing blue gloves preparing for a blood smear procedure. The individual has an EDTA blood sample in a tube with a purple stopper in their left hand and arranges glass slides on a white countertop in a row. The text on the blood tube reads "15 3861 Equivet" which refers to the identifier and the veterinary company that produced it. The person then gently mixes the blood sample in the tube. They then take a wooden applicator stick and run it through the blood sample to check for any clots that may have adhered. All of this takes place in a lab-like setting.

The video segment features a person wearing a light blue gown with a white undershirt and blue gloves performing lab procedures. At the beginning of the clip, the person holds a package of "Fisherbrand Frosted Beveled Edge Microscope Slides Precleaned" in their gloved hands, highlighting the importance of using microscope slides to make blood smears. They emphasize the near impossibility of making good blood smears without them. The video then transitions to the person extracting blood from a PCV tube with a small capillary tube to apply drops of blood to three microscope slides. The narrator points out that the first drop that was added to the first slide was too small, and that the second drop put on the second slide was too large and that the final drops put on the third slide were just right. The background is a white, gridded surface with several microscope slides visible. The camera is mostly static, providing clear views of the items and the person's movements.

Okay, here is a description of the video segment.

The video shows a person with both hands visible, wearing blue gloves, on a white, patterned surface. In the shot are three microscope slides with a small drop of red blood on each. In addition, the person has a glass tube with red liquid in it, as well as a clear microscope slide that is used as a spreader. The speaker is explaining different ways people make blood smears on slides, and demonstrates each method on one of the slides. For example, the person demonstrates the Olympic ski jump technique in which the spreader leaves the slide, resulting in a cytology slide, or a line preparation. Also, the person uses both sides of a slide to increase its usage. Another poor blood smearing method demonstrated is going slowly, which results in spreading the blood right off the slide. Finally, the person also uses the race car rev method in which the spreader is moved back and forth, which wastes time and makes the operator anxious. At the end, only one smear is made.

Alright, here's a description of the video segment:

The video displays a gloved hand applying a drop of blood to a microscope slide. Another slide lays nearby on a white surface. First, the gloved hand applies the slide to the drop of blood, then drags it horizontally. She remarks that people often pull instead of push to make their smears. She says that this leads to interesting shapes and less control. Then she grabs another clean slide, applies it to a new drop of blood, and smears this one. She says that if you press down too hard on the bottom side, you'll get uneven production. Then, she grabs another slide to create a third smear. The slide shakes, resulting in a wobbly smear. The video ends with a blank microscope slide being displayed.

The video segment shows a person in a lab coat and blue gloves demonstrating how to prepare blood slides. The person carefully places three small drops of blood, one on each of the three transparent rectangular glass slides lying on top of a white absorbent cloth. Using another glass slide as a spreader, the person anchors each slide with their index finger, carefully avoiding pressing the middle of the slide, and spreads the blood by quickly pushing the spreader across the slide. The person uses another spare glass slide to spread the blood on the remaining slide. The person holds the end of the spare glass slide and the blood smear slide between the index finger and the spare glass slide.

The video segment shows a person in a medical setting wearing blue medical gloves carefully handling blood samples on glass slides. The person is shown placing these slides into blue and pink containers, presumably for safe storage or transportation. The slides contain what appears to be red blood smears. Throughout the video, the camera focuses on the slides and the containers. The background appears to be a white, sterile medical workspace. The gloves are being used to protect the specimens from dirt, flies, water, slides from each other, and, if mailing them, bubble wrap, so they don’t accidentally get damaged.
The speaker says that “TOP” is marked on one of the cases.

The video shows a close-up of a laboratory setting. At the start, a gloved hand places a glass slide on a white surface. The slide has a dark purple stain on it, and a label, which reads "R.I. Smear 1:2". Then, the camera zooms out to show six different glass slides laid out on a white surface. Each slide has a purple smear on it, and a white label. From left to right, the labels read: "D09 C 01142", "15 C 28451", "D07 F 33943", "D09 C 24927", "D08 F 21331", and "15 C 38426". After that, the text beneath the slides identify each smear. From left to right they read: "2 smears on one", "Too thick", "Squash prep", "Too thin", "Flies!", and "Good smear". Finally, the text, “Examples of 5 Poor Smears and One Good Blood Smear” is revealed at the bottom of the slides. The background is a simple white, presumably the lab bench.
